summary: The draft is technically dense but systematically stops one level above the corpus on the four topics the query names most directly. The projection method is described as a two-sentence sketch without the theorem that makes it constructible; the complexity claims travel without their number-of-goods qualifier; every efficiency index in the report is quoted without power or predictive success, and the one power sentence in the draft points the wrong way; the CCEI-equals-1 loophole is declared closed when the corpus shows its hypothesis fails on the exact designs the field uses; and three of the report's load-bearing empirical anchors (POISE's 20.15%/0%, RankFusion's NDCG gain, the 'no dose-response exists' claim) are contradicted or hollowed out by depth notes the draft did not use.

findings.location: §2C 'The repair layer, and its one missing cell' — the sentence 'The parallel object for perturbing *quantities* — the agent's actual choices — is named in two sentences, with no inequalities, no program, no complexity classification'; and the parallel sentence in §9C's first open cell.
findings.issue: The draft reports that the Average Quantity Error is only a sketch, but omits the single technical fact that makes the missing cell actionable and that the corpus establishes in full: the multiplier-free characterisation whose inequalities are linear in quantities, so promoting the bundle to a decision variable keeps the program a MILP. As written the reader cannot tell whether the cell is empty because the problem is hard or because nobody wrote it down. The corpus says the latter, and says exactly why.
findings.evidence: docs/METHOD_NOTE_Q3.md §'Demuynck & Rehbeck (2023) — the key source; read in full': their Theorem 2 drops the Afriat multipliers entirely and characterises GARP by ordinal levels u_t ∈ [0,1] with 'p_t·q_t ≥ p_t·q_v ⇒ u_t ≥ u_v' and 'p_t·q_t > p_t·q_v ⇒ u_t > u_v', encoded with binaries U_{t,v}; the note quotes them: 'the inequalities (IP-1)-(IP-4) are linear in utility numbers, prices, and quantities.' The verbatim AQE sketch is also in that note: 'one needs to introduce variables q̃_t ∈ R^K_+ and define GARP consistency conditional on these bundles. The Average Quantity Error (AQE) would then consist of minimizing the mean of the errors ‖q_t − q̃_t‖ conditional on (p_t, q̃_t)_{t≤T} satisfying GARP.' The same note's opening establishes the contrast: with the data fixed the Afriat inequalities are already an LP; the bilinearity is created 'entirely by promoting x̃ to a decision variable, which turns λ_j·p_j·x̃_i into a product of two unknowns', and 'fixing the ordering does not linearise the projection problem'.
findings.recommendation: In §2C, after naming the AQE sketch, add two or three sentences of actual content: quote the two-sentence AQE definition verbatim; state that the same paper's Theorem 2 replaces Afriat's utility-and-multiplier pair with ordinal levels in [0,1] plus binary comparison indicators, making every constraint linear jointly in utilities, prices AND quantities; and draw the consequence the draft currently leaves implicit — that because the inequalities are linear in quantities, promoting the bundle to a decision variable keeps the program a mixed-integer linear program with no bilinear term, whereas the naive Afriat route is bilinear the moment the bundle becomes a variable and stays bilinear even with the ordering fixed. Then correct §9C: the obstruction to the missing cell is not tractability, it is well-posedness (see the non-closedness finding).

findings.location: §3C 'What this front has and has not done' — 'The post-hoc cell is thin not because nobody thought of enforcing GARP on an agent, but because the corresponding economics program was never written down'; and §6A's 'Excluded, and why' list of economics operators never aimed at an artificial agent; and §9C's first open cell.
findings.issue: The draft's causal explanation for the empty cell — that the economics program was never written down — is falsified by a named, published algorithm in the corpus that does exactly minimal perturbation of chosen bundles onto the GARP-consistent set. Omitting it makes the report's central 'missing cell' claim look broader than the evidence supports, and it drops the one prior work a reader in this literature would ask about first.
findings.evidence: docs/METHOD_NOTE_Q3.md quotes the Smeulders–Crama–Spieksma (2019) EJOR survey directly: 'The problem of finding these minimally different rationalizable datasets can be formulated as a non-linear optimization problem, which, in general, is hard to solve. To avoid solving large scale non-linear problems, De Peretti (2005) approaches this problem with an iterative procedure. Working on garp, his algorithm tackles violations one at a time, also perturbing only one observation at a time. [...] While this algorithm does not guarantee an optimal solution, it allows handling large datasets, especially if the number of violations is small.' The same note (§'the recommended formulation's fallback') describes the mechanism: 'for a cycle between x_i and x_j, compute the minimal perturbation that removes the violation under each of the two orientations, take the cheaper, update the dataset, re-test GARP, repeat' — De Peretti, C. (2005), Macroeconomic Dynamics 9(3), 372–397. The note's fetch record flags that the primary was not obtained and the description is sourced to the 2019 survey.
findings.recommendation: Add De Peretti (2005) to §2C as the one existing heuristic operator for the quantity-perturbation problem, with its mechanism (one violation at a time, one observation at a time, cheaper of the two cycle orientations) and its stated failure mode (no optimality guarantee), attributing the characterisation to the 2019 algorithmic survey since the primary was not retrieved. Add it to the §6A exclusion list under 'existing as operators but never aimed at an artificial agent'. Then narrow §3C and §9C: what is missing is not the program but the exact, budget-constrained, complexity-classified version of it — and any application to an artificial agent.

findings.location: §2B 'The severity layer and its computational stratification' — 'Deleting relations at minimum cost is NP-hard, by reduction from maximum acyclic subgraph [23]. The Houtman–Maks and average Varian indices are likewise NP-hard [15].' Also §9C's 'deletion is polynomial at two goods'.
findings.issue: The draft states the hardness results without the number-of-goods qualifier that makes them true or false, and §9C asserts the two-goods polynomiality with no source and no matching three-goods result. Every LLM budget-set study the report discusses runs at two goods, which is precisely the regime where the flat 'Houtman–Maks is NP-hard' claim is wrong. The corpus has the threshold result, the reduction used, and the inapproximability statement.
findings.evidence: docs/METHOD_NOTE_Q3.md §'Boodaghians & Vetta (2015), arXiv:1507.07581 / WINE 2015 — read in full' quotes them: 'for two-commodity markets the consumer rationality problem is polynomial time solvable; we prove this via a reduction to the vertex cover problem on perfect graphs. For three-commodity markets, however, the problem is NP-complete.' The note adds: 'In general the deletion problem is equivalent in approximation to directed feedback vertex set' and 'Houtman–Maks is NP-hard is false at K = 2. Any complexity claim the paper makes must carry its K.' The same note's §'Smeulders, Spieksma, Cherchye & De Rock (2014)' records that Varian's vector index and Houtman–Maks are NP-hard, that 'no constant-factor polynomial-time approximation exists for either, unless P = NP', and that 'hardness is obtained by reduction from independent set'. On the minimum-cost side, docs/METHOD_NOTE_Q3.md §'Dean & Martin (2016)' records the reduction to the maximal acyclic set problem and its equivalence to minimum set covering, with their brute-force count: 'with only twenty observations there are over a million combinations to check, and with 40 there are more than 1 × 10¹²'.
findings.recommendation: In §2B, attach the goods dimension to each hardness claim: state that the Houtman–Maks deletion problem is polynomial-time solvable at two commodities (by reduction to vertex cover on perfect graphs) and NP-complete at three, that in general it is approximation-equivalent to directed feedback vertex set, and that Varian's vector index and Houtman–Maks admit no constant-factor polynomial-time approximation unless P = NP with hardness by reduction from independent set. Note explicitly that the two-good regime is the one every LLM budget-set study operates in, so the hardness picture as usually quoted does not bind there. In §9C, cite the two-goods/three-goods threshold rather than asserting the polynomial half unsourced.

findings.location: §2C, the paragraph beginning 'That object is named elsewhere, and the naming matters' — the non-closedness discussion and the sentence 'for the Varian, swaps and least-squares losses, if the data violate GARP then the set of minimising well-behaved utility functions is *empty*, so the infimum is approached but not attained'.
findings.issue: The draft states non-closedness and non-attainment but drops the operationally decisive consequence: the natural minimal-perturbation index can read exactly zero on data that violate the axiom. That is the failure mode a practitioner would actually hit — an operator that reports 'no repair needed' on a dataset that needs repair — and it is the strongest single reason the missing cell is missing. The named boundary objects and the two escape routes are also stated more loosely than the corpus states them.
findings.evidence: docs/METHOD_NOTE_Q3.md §'Chen, Lanier & Quah (arXiv:2405.08464) — read in full; the most dangerous source for this project': 'Proposition 1: no goodness-of-fit index is both continuous and accurate. The reason is structural: "the datasets which obey GARP do not form a closed set." One can build GARP-obeying D_n → D̄ with D̄ violating GARP. They call such boundary cases cusp datasets.' And the consequence, stated in the note in bold: 'the LS index can report a distance of exactly 0 for a dataset that violates GARP, and since the feasible set {x̃ : (p, x̃) satisfies GARP} is not closed, the infimum need not be attained by any x̃.' Their Proposition 7 makes the Afriat, Varian, Swaps and Least Squares loss functions 'accurate but not minimizable — argmin is empty — with Houtman–Maks the only exception'; Proposition 11 characterises the classes admitting accurate and minimizable losses as exactly those whose rationalisable datasets form a closed set, with the homothetic class and the expected-utility class with concave Bernoulli functions shown to qualify.
findings.recommendation: Add the exact-zero failure mode as its own sentence in §2C: the least-squares projection distance can be exactly 0 on a dataset that violates GARP, because the GARP-consistent set is not closed and the violating dataset sits at a limit point. Name the boundary objects as 'cusp datasets'. Attach the proposition numbers so the escapes are checkable (Prop. 1 for the impossibility, Prop. 7 for the empty argmin, Prop. 11 for the closed-class characterisation), and make clear that the two escapes are the homothetic class and expected utility with a concave Bernoulli function, not merely 'restrict to homothetic preferences or expected utility'.

findings.location: §3A 'The measurement wave, which is the contrast class' — 'obtained in two-good settings with few budget sets, a regime of limited test power that the apparatus's leading advocate concedes in his own review [30][7]'.
findings.issue: This is the draft's only statement about test power and it points the wrong way. The corpus shows that the two-good, 25-budget-set design is the HIGH-power regime, with unconditional power measured at 99.9% and independently replicated at 100%; power falls exponentially in the number of GOODS, not from having only two. The paper cited runs four separate power analyses, and its genuine power caveat is a different statistic entirely — conditional/bootstrap power — which the draft does not mention. Since §3A is the report's characterisation of the entire measurement wave, and §7F later builds a headroom argument on the same index values, a mis-stated power claim propagates.
findings.evidence: audit/killcheck_E3.md: 'Bronars (1987) power. Simulated subjects choose uniformly at random along each budget line, 25 choices... 99.9% of simulated subjects violate GARP. I replicated this independently against the paper's stated generator (1,000 simulated subjects): 100.0% violation rate, mean CCEI 0.718, median 0.727, 95th percentile 0.902.' Predictive success for the model over the random benchmark: '94.9%, 88.9%, 80.9%, 91.9%'; Selten scores 0.279–0.281. The real caveat is separate: 'Bootstrap power (Andreoni–Miller 2002; 10,000 synthetic subjects resampling choices from the actual DM pool at each budget). Here the probability of rejecting GARP is 7.9%, 26.3%, 26.0%, 8.5% for the model versus 95.4%, 96.6%, 99.8%, 99.8% for humans... attributed to the model's low preference heterogeneity.' The direction of the dimensionality effect is in audit/BRONARS_NOTE.md §'The dimensionality trap': Crawford & Tian (2026, arXiv:2605.29361) prove Selten's Area A_K ≥ 1 − C_T·exp(−c₁K), so power → 0 as K grows — 'T = 10: Area exceeds 0.9 by K = 9... K = 24, T = 10: Area 0.9996 — power 0.0004' — and 'Two goods is not a limitation of this project's design; at n = 25–50 it is the reason the design works.' That paper is in the vault as note 260529361-the-empirical-content-of-revealed-preference-in-high-dimensions and is cited nowhere in the draft.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the power clause in §3A. State that the leading budget-set design reports 99.9% Bronars power on its 25 two-good budget sets (independently replicated at 100%, mean simulated CCEI 0.718), so the two-good setting is the high-power regime rather than a low-power one; that unconditional power falls exponentially in the number of goods and additional observations do not recover it, citing the high-dimensions result already in the vault (Area ≥ 1 − C_T·exp(−c₁K); Area 0.9996 at K = 24, T = 10); and that the paper's own conceded weakness is conditional bootstrap power of 7.9–26.3% for the model against 95.4–99.8% for humans, a statement about the model's preference homogeneity rather than about the budget sets. Add the vault note on high-dimensional revealed preference to the source list.

findings.location: Every place the draft quotes an efficiency index without a power figure: §3A ('CCEI averages above 0.997'), §3B ('the correlation between an individual's efficiency index and the gain they receive is 0.456'), §7F ('an 8B open-weight model's from 0.953 to 0.841'; 'flagship efficiency indices already sit at 0.994 to 1.000'), §9C ('transitivity indices of 0.957 to 1.000').
findings.issue: The corpus contains an explicit standing rule that no efficiency index is interpretable without the power of the design that produced it, together with the identity that converts a pass rate into an interpretable quantity and two published calibration numbers. The draft reports index values throughout as if they were self-interpreting. This is the single most repeated depth gap in the report.
findings.evidence: audit/BRONARS_NOTE.md states the rule and the identity: 'Any CCEI number this project ever reports must be paired with the Bronars power of the budget sets that produced it, because a high CCEI under low test power means "the test could not have failed", not "the agent is rational"'; 'area a = 1 − Bronars power (Beatty & Crawford 2011, §3); predictive success m = pass rate − area = pass rate + Bronars power − 1 (Selten 1991)'; and 'Bronars power costs nothing to compute. It depends only on the prices and budgets — the agent's choices never enter it — so it can and must be computed before a single API call is spent.' The canonical calibration: 'Beatty & Crawford's Spanish household panel: a GARP pass rate of 0.957... against a relative area of 0.912, meaning the test had only 8.8 % power. Corrected predictive success: 0.045', with their words 'out-performed a random number generator - but only by 4.5%'. The threshold version: 'on the Andreoni–Miller altruism design, Andreoni, Gillen & Harbaugh (2013, Table 1) report that 69 % of uniform-random simulated subjects had CCEI below 0.99 — meaning 31 % of pure random agents would have cleared a CCEI-0.99 bar on that design.'
findings.recommendation: Add a short, explicitly methodological passage — best placed at the end of §2B or as the opening of §7F — stating that an efficiency index is a statistic on a test and carries information only in proportion to that test's power; give the identity predictive success = pass rate − (1 − power); give the Spanish-panel calibration (pass rate 0.957, area 0.912, power 8.8%, corrected predictive success 0.045) and the threshold calibration (31% of uniform-random agents clear a CCEI of 0.99 on a published altruism design, mean simulated CCEI 0.88); and note that power depends only on prices and budgets, so it is computable before any data are collected. Then, wherever the draft quotes near-1 index values as evidence of coherence, add the qualifier that no power figure accompanies them in the source.

findings.location: §3B 'Label-free regularization, specified and unrun' — 'A supporting lemma closes the known CCEI loophole: with prices drawn from continuous densities and budget-exhausting choices, CCEI equals 1 if and only if GARP holds, with probability one [7].'
findings.issue: The draft declares the loophole closed. The corpus shows the lemma is a distributional guarantee about a sampler, not a property of the estimator, and that its hypothesis fails on the exact design the LLM literature the report surveys actually uses. The corpus also has numerically verified false-positive rates. As written, the draft licenses the reader to treat an index reading of 1.0 as a certificate of GARP on data where it is not one.
findings.evidence: docs/METHOD_NOTE_Q6.md: the design the field inherits 'specifies its price parameters as M, N ∈ [0.1, 1] with max{M, N} ≥ 0.5 and — in the same footnote, in every condition including the baseline — "We keep two decimals." That is a 91-point discrete price grid with no Lebesgue density... the hypothesis of Lemma 1 fails on the design the project inherits.' Measured tie frequencies at T = 25, K = 2, prices on a grid in [1,5]: integer prices give 7.3% of ordered pairs as exact ties and '100 %' of datasets containing at least one tie; two-decimal prices 0.04% / 20%; continuous prices 0.00% / 0%. Measured false certificates over uniform-random agents (S = 1500, T = 8, exact arithmetic): on integer prices P(GARP fails) = 0.674, P(CCEI > 0.99) = 0.515, and P(CCEI = 1 exactly AND GARP fails) = 0.189, against 0.000 for continuous prices. Cross-check: 'Across 63,200 continuous-price replications there were 12,102 genuine GARP failures and not one exact CCEI of 1.0.' And the trap returns for realistic agents: 'a T = 25 agent targeting a fixed budget share with ±1 grid-step noise on a quarter-point price grid shows P(CCEI = 1 and GARP fails) = 8.7 %, against 0.0 % for the same agent on continuous prices.'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the lemma sentence so it carries its hypothesis and its scope. State that the equivalence holds only when prices are drawn independently from Lebesgue densities with budget-exhausting choices; that the guarantee is about a sampler, not an estimator, so it says nothing about data a researcher is handed; that the published LLM budget-set design keeps prices to two decimals and therefore fails the hypothesis; and give at least the two headline verified numbers — 100% of 25-observation integer-price designs contain at least one exact budget-equality tie, and 18.9% of uniform-random agents on integer prices report an exact index of 1.0 while genuinely violating GARP, against zero such events in 63,200 continuous-price replications carrying 12,102 real GARP failures. Add the near-rational T = 25 figure (8.7% on quarter-point prices) since that is the regime an agent experiment actually operates in.

findings.location: §7F 'Can the instrument bear the inference?' — the closing argument 'if the headroom to *create* variation in coherence lives in small models while flagship indices sit at 0.994 to 1.000, the lever needed to dose a frontier agent may not exist'.
findings.issue: This conclusion treats near-1 index values as behaviourally near-perfect, and the corpus establishes two reasons that reading is wrong — severe compression of the index near 1, and a large threshold-slack false-clear rate at exactly the 0.99 bar the draft is reasoning about. The same corpus also contains a direct demonstration of headroom in the very models the draft calls format-stable, produced by holding budget sets fixed and changing only wording. The draft's own §3A already concedes framing sensitivity but does not carry the numbers here, so §7F ends on a conclusion its own evidence base contradicts.
findings.evidence: audit/killcheck_E3.md: 'CCEI compresses near 1. A mean of 0.997 corresponds to a genuinely noisy optimiser, not to a perfect one.' The calibration sweep of a CES maximiser with Gaussian allocation noise: sd 3 → mean CCEI 0.9999, sd 5 → 0.9984 (21.3% GARP violation), sd 12 → 0.9625 (78.3% violation), so 'the observed 0.997-0.999 is what a near-deterministic optimiser with roughly 3-5 points of allocation noise produces, and the human 0.963-0.985 is what roughly 8-12 points produces... the 0.003 of apparent headroom between 0.997 and 1.000 is not 0.3% of the available behavioural range — it is the compressed image of a real and non-trivial residual inconsistency.' On headroom: 'Holding the budget sets fixed and changing only how prices are worded, mean CCEI falls to 0.698-0.901; changing only continuous-to-discrete, to 0.780-0.908. Between 32% and 88% of runs land below 0.9', and '19% of social-preference runs violate GARP at the paper's best condition; 5-11% in the others.' On threshold slack, docs/METHOD_NOTE_Q6.md: for a T = 25 near-rational agent, P(GARP fails and CCEI > 0.99) is 31.8% on quarter-point prices, of which 23.1 points is threshold slack, and 29.0% even on continuous prices.
findings.recommendation: Qualify the no-headroom conclusion in §7F with three corpus facts. First, the index compresses near 1: a mean of 0.997 corresponds to an optimiser carrying roughly 3–5 points of allocation noise on a 100-point budget, and the human 0.963–0.985 band to 8–12 — a factor of two to three in behavioural noise compressed into 0.03 index units. Second, headroom demonstrably exists in the same models: holding budget sets fixed and changing only price wording drops mean CCEI to 0.698–0.901 and discretisation to 0.780–0.908, with 32–88% of runs below 0.9, and 19% of runs violating GARP outright at the best condition. Third, a near-rational agent at 25 observations still trips a CCEI > 0.99 clear while violating GARP roughly 29–32% of the time, so the flagship 0.994–1.000 band is not a certificate. Conclude that the lever is presentational rather than absent, which is also what the report's own §3A framing sensitivity implies.

findings.location: §5B 'The accepters, and what their numbers actually show' and §9B 'Half two: populated but unidentified' — specifically 'or the treatment is binary rather than graded, so no dose–response curve exists to read', and §9C's second open cell.
findings.issue: The draft asserts that no dose–response curve exists in this literature. Two are published, one of them a nine-level sweep against a downstream generation metric, and it points in the direction most relevant to the query's second half: more weight on the transitive component improves downstream quality up to an interior optimum, and the cyclic-first direction is monotonically worse. Omitting it leaves the report's answer to 'has the relationship been empirically tested, in either direction?' weaker than the corpus supports, and leaves the §9C novelty claim overstated. The same interim note also contains the sharpest quantitative version of the capacity confound the draft argues for in §5B.
findings.evidence: audit/ITEM2_occupants_C.md §B.6 and §'Is a dose–response curve already published?': 'Nine levels of λ ∈ {−2, −1, −0.5, 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 2}, where λ sets the early-training weight on the transitive component relative to the cyclic one, traced against AlpacaEval 2.0 length-controlled win rate at iteration 3. Inverted U, interior optimum at λ = +1.0 (41.90), monotone decline into the cyclic-first regime (40.21 → 38.66 → 37.27), decline again at the extreme transitive tilt (+2.0 → 40.15). Span 4.63 points. Length flat across the sweep, so not a verbosity artifact. This is a published dose–response between degree of transitivity emphasis and downstream generation quality... and it favours transitivity.' Limits recorded in the same note: 'Single run per λ, no seeds, no CI, one benchmark, one iteration index', the endpoints 'pure BT' and 'pure GPM' are not on the curve, and λ is not a coherence measure. The weak second curve: 'GPM Table 2... five levels of embedding dimension d ∈ {1, 2, 4, 6, 8} with d = 1 exactly equal to the fully transitive BT model... non-monotone with an interior optimum at d = 6'. §B.5 of the same note supplies the capacity-confound numbers: independently retrained BT scores 79.76 against the 74.85 the original reported, turning a +7.44 margin into +1.23 ('roughly five sixths of GPM's headline advantage evaporates'), and on the newer reward benchmark at 8B 'BT 70.10 vs GPM(2) 70.08 vs GPM(4) 69.69 — BT beats both cycle-tolerant arms'.
findings.recommendation: In §5B or §7, add the nine-level λ sweep as a published dose–response result, with its shape (inverted U, interior optimum at λ = +1.0, monotone decline into the cyclic-first regime), its span (4.63 LC win-rate points), its verbosity control (response length flat, 2139–2245), and its limits (one run per point, no seeds or CIs, one benchmark, endpoints not on the curve, λ is a schedule tilt rather than a quantity of coherence). Add the five-level embedding-dimension sweep as the weak companion, noting that d = 1 is exactly the transitive model. Then rewrite §9B's third disjunct and §9C's second open cell so the novelty claim is about the object (an agent's own choices), the dose metric (a coherence index) and the outcome (an exogenous payoff) — not about the bare fact of varying a degree. While in §5B, replace or supplement the 'nine wins to eight' framing with the baseline-strength numbers (74.85 → 79.76 retrained BT; +7.44 → +1.23), which state the capacity confound quantitatively, and correct the description of the +1.23% margin: it is the transitive-plus-cyclic decomposition over the best cycle-tolerant arm, i.e. a pro-transitivity number, with the margin over the scalar model being +1.70.

findings.location: §7A 'The positives, ranked by exogeneity of the outcome' — 'Rank fusion raises NDCG@10 by more than six points against human relevance labels [52]'; the §6A table row 4; and §6B's count of four exogenous-metric entries.
findings.issue: The draft counts this system as one of only four entries scored on an exogenous metric and uses it to support the §7C rule about target alignment. The corpus shows the transitivity-targeting component of that system contributes essentially nothing to the exogenous metric, that transitivity is never re-measured after the repair, and that the headline gain comes from a positional-bias correction rather than from a coherence axiom. One of the report's four load-bearing positives is therefore not evidence for the proposition it is cited for.
findings.evidence: audit/ITEM2_occupants_A.md §'Three findings that the prior summary missed': '(i) Transitive inconsistency is never re-measured after repair. Table 2's caption states outright that "This tournament graph is constructed from the comparisons without ICL and calibration." No post-repair triad count appears anywhere in the paper.' '(ii) The component that targets transitivity contributes essentially nothing to the exogenous metric. Aggregation across sorters (Table 7, DL19): for D1, best single sorter 70.57 ± 0.35 → aggregated 70.58 ± 0.45, a gain of +0.01. For P2, 74.75 → 75.04 (+0.29). For D5, best single 70.88 → aggregated 69.76, i.e. worse... Essentially the entire headline NDCG gain comes from ICL + calibration, which attack positional bias — a framing/measurement artefact of the elicitation, not a coherence axiom in the revealed-preference sense.' '(iii) Repair sometimes hurts... E2 loses −2.49 from ICL alone and −0.10 from calibration alone; D2 loses −0.81 from ICL alone.' And on the comparison the paper's prose omits: 'on DL20 the repaired pairwise ranker (65.10) does not beat the listwise baseline (65.49).' The same note records the citable refusal: the authors name 'Kemeny rank aggregation' and reject it because such methods 'are either NP-hard or not specifically designed for list aggregation', which the note calls 'a published, citable statement that the minimal-perturbation route was available and was not taken.'
findings.recommendation: In §7A, keep the NDCG figure but attach its decomposition: the gain is attributable to in-context ordering and calibration, which correct positional bias, while the multi-ranker aggregation that targets transitivity moves the metric by +0.01 on the cell the headline comes from and by −1.12 on another; individual components lose up to 2.49 points; the paper never re-measures transitivity after the repair (its triad counts are computed on unrepaired comparisons); and on the second benchmark the repaired pairwise ranker does not beat the listwise baseline. Adjust the §6A table's 'Reported sign' and §6B's exogenous-metric count accordingly, and revisit the §7C rule, which currently treats this entry as a same-target success. Separately, move the explicit Kemeny refusal into §8B as documentary evidence that the minimal-perturbation route was seen and declined on tractability grounds.

findings.location: Opening paragraph ('provably driving score-pair reversal conflicts to exactly 0% [3]'), §5A 'Training-time score repair by isotonic projection' ('from 20.15% to exactly 0%, where inference-time probabilistic aggregation on the same corpus retains 20.46%'), and §7A ('overall benchmark score reaches 77.96... 10.13 points above the strongest open baseline, and whose signal produces better embodied manipulation policies').
findings.issue: Four separate over-readings of the report's flagship enforcement result, all corrected in the corpus. The 20.15%/20.46% pair exists only in the source's abstract and appears nowhere in its body. The quality theorem the draft calls the strongest in the corpus does not apply to the object actually used as a training label, because of a rounding step the source itself concedes is not a metric projection. The 10.13-point margin is against a different training recipe, not against the projection's own control. And the downstream test is video generation judged by human preference, not robot policy execution.
findings.evidence: audit/ITEM2_occupants_A.md §'Two evidentiary faults': '(a) The abstract's central theoretical claim is unsubstantiated in the body. "POISE provably reduces training-corpus score-pair reversal conflicts from 20.15% to 0%, whereas TrustJudge still retains 20.46%"... Those two figures appear only in the abstract. A full-text scan of all 23 pages, all seven tables, and Appendices A–F finds neither number anywhere else. η_cross = 0 is a definitional consequence of the projection and is proved; the empirical 20.15% pre-repair rate and the 20.46% comparator are asserted and never shown.' §'Where it is not the same mathematical object as a GARP projection': 'Quantisation breaks the guarantee. Remark 1 concedes that round-half-up "is not a metric projection onto a convex set" and bounds the extra error by √m / 2 ≤ 0.87 — on a 1-to-5 scale, that is up to 22% of the full range. The proved theorem applies to ŝ′, the object that is not used as the training label'; and 'Dimension m ≤ 3. Every projection in the paper is over at most three numbers.' §'Exact numbers, with baselines': 'But 10.13 is not the effect of the projection. RoboReward-4B is a different training recipe... The matched comparison for POISE is raw-distillation SFT on the same four-paradigm corpus: 77.09 → 77.96, i.e. +0.87 Overall — and that +0.87 requires the additional RL stage.' §'The downstream test is not what the ledger says it is' quotes the paper's own Limitations: 'our downstream validation is based on video generation and human preference comparison rather than closed-loop policy execution on physical robots', with n = 68, no confidence interval and no significance test.
findings.recommendation: Four targeted qualifications. (1) Where the 20.15% → 0% and 20.46% figures appear, note that the zero is a definitional consequence of the projection and is proved, while the empirical pre-repair rate and its comparator appear only in the source's abstract and are not substantiated anywhere in its body — and drop them from the lede's list of demonstrated results or mark them as abstract-only. (2) Where the quality theorem is called the strongest theoretical result in the corpus, add that the source's own Remark concedes the round-half-up step back to the integer scale is not a metric projection and bounds the extra error at up to 0.87 on a 1-to-5 scale, so the theorem holds for an object that is not the deployed training label; and note that every projection in the paper is over at most three numbers. (3) In §7A replace or qualify the 10.13-point figure with the matched comparison of +0.87 against raw distillation on the same corpus, noting that even that requires the subsequent reinforcement stage — which is consistent with the draft's own §7D dissociation. (4) Replace 'better embodied manipulation policies' with the accurate description: 68 human-judged head-to-head comparisons of generated videos, no confidence interval, no closed-loop physical execution, per the paper's own limitations.

findings.location: §7B 'The three failures' ('the Houtman–Maks index down by 0.262'), §7C ('Its own authors note that a prior study found revision *does* raise consistency, and concede that effectiveness depends on the configuration of the choice interface'), and §7F's reliability paragraph.
findings.issue: The Houtman–Maks delta is stated with the right number but no unit, so it reads as an effect an order of magnitude larger than the efficiency-index delta printed beside it, when the corpus says it is a nothing. The report also rests a substantial claim — 'three independent negatives establish a real adverse prior' — on deltas that carry no inferential statistic at all, which the corpus flags explicitly as the soft spot of that negative. The authors' actual concession is stronger and more quotable than the draft's paraphrase, and the same source contains a practice effect that bears directly on the null-operator control the draft calls for in §9C.
findings.evidence: audit/ITEM2_occupants_B.md §'(2) The repair intervention': the deltas are ΔCCEI −0.025 / −0.013 and ΔHMI −0.262 / −0.058, followed by three honesty notes: '1. HMI is a count. ΔHMI = −0.262 out of 40 trials is a quarter of one trial. It is not a backfire; it is a nothing. 2. ΔCCEI = −0.025 is not nothing... 3. No inferential test is reported. The paper gives descriptive means only — no p-value, no CI, no test statistic on any of the four deltas. This is a descriptive null on n = 97, not a powered equivalence test.' The authors' own words, quoted in the note: 'due to the ineffectiveness of the intervention, we cannot rule out that a more effective intervention could increase the reliability of rationality measurements.' Same note §'(1)': 'The range recorded... as "ICC 0.07–0.55" is wrong at the top end. The true range across every estimate in the paper is 0.071 to 0.685 (CCEI tops out at 0.626, HMI at 0.685)... Not one of the ~40 ICC estimates reported in the paper reaches 0.75.' Same note §'(3)': 'there is a practice effect. Participants became measurably more rational at the second measurement (study 1: b = 0.023, SE = 0.017, t(240.93) = 1.387, p = 0.167; study 2: b = 0.037, SE = 0.02, t(658.25) = 3.183, p = 0.002)', and the sharpest sentence, 'taking individual measurements of CCEI and HMI yielded approximately two times worse predictive accuracy for another measurement within the same individual than simply assuming the population mean.'
findings.recommendation: In §7B, give the Houtman–Maks delta its unit — the index is a count of jointly rationalizable trials out of 40, so −0.262 is roughly a quarter of one trial and is not a backfire — and state that no p-value, confidence interval or test statistic is reported on any of the four deltas, making this a descriptive null on 97 participants rather than a powered equivalence test. In §7C, replace the paraphrase with the authors' actual concession about not being able to rule out that a more effective intervention would work. In §7F, tighten the reliability numbers to the corpus's corrected range (0.071–0.685 across roughly forty estimates, with CCEI topping out at 0.626 and Houtman–Maks at 0.685, none reaching 0.75) and add the practice effect (index rises on re-measurement, b = 0.037, p = 0.002) plus the population-mean comparison — an individual measurement predicts that individual's next measurement about twice as badly as simply assuming the population mean. The practice effect should be cross-referenced in §9C, since it is a concrete reason a before/after repair design needs the distance-matched null-operator control the draft is asking for.
